summary.text: An extinction event is a widespread and rapid decrease in the biodiversity on Earth.
It is identified by a sharp fall in the diversity and abundance of multicellular organisms.
It occurs when the rate of extinction rises above both the background extinction rate and the rate of speciation.

facts.label: Number of events
facts.value: Estimates range from five to over twenty in 540 million years

facts.label: The Big Five
facts.value: Appear to be the largest of a smooth continuum of events

facts.label: The Great Dying
facts.value: Largest extinction of the Phanerozoic, at the Permian-Triassic transition

facts.label: Great Dying toll
facts.value: About 81% of all marine species died

items.prompt: Species disappear at about the usual background rate, and new species form at the usual rate. Is that an extinction event?

options.label: Yes; any loss of species counts as an event
No; the extinction rate must rise above both of those rates
Yes, once the losses have lasted more than a century
No; only the loss of plants counts as an event

items.explain: An extinction event occurs when the rate of extinction increases with respect to the background extinction rate and the rate of speciation.

items.prompt: Two scientists count different numbers of major mass extinctions in the last 540 million years. What explains the gap?

options.label: Some extinctions in the record turned out never to have happened
Only five ever happened, and the rest are mistakes in dating
The fossils from some periods are too well preserved to read
They disagree on what counts as major and on which diversity data to use

items.explain: Estimates range from five to more than twenty because of disagreement about what constitutes a major extinction event and about the data chosen to measure past diversity.

items.prompt: When the Great Dying emptied many ecological niches on land, which group gained an opportunity to diversify?

options.label: Archosaurs, the relatives of dinosaurs and crocodiles
Synapsids, the relatives of mammals
Trilobites, the marine arthropods
Placoderms, the armored fish

items.explain: The recovery of vertebrates took 30 million years, but the vacant niches created the opportunity for archosaurs to diversify, while many synapsid lineages were cut short.

items.prompt: Fossil pollen and spores from some plant communities show little or short-lived disturbance across the Great Dying. What might this suggest about life on land?

options.label: Land ecosystems were wiped out entirely
Plants were harmed more than animals
Land ecosystems may have suffered less than once believed
Pollen cannot survive as a fossil

items.explain: The extinction's impact on land ecosystems may have been less severe than once believed, since fossil pollen and spores indicate minimal or short-lived disruption for some plant communities.

items.prompt: In the explanation many scientists favour, rivers wash land nutrients into the sea and cause huge algal blooms. How did that lead to mass extinction?

options.label: The algae gave off a poison that killed the reef animals directly
The blooms blocked all sunlight from reaching the seabed
The algae overgrew the corals until they starved of food
The dying algae decomposed and used up dissolved oxygen, leaving water anoxic

items.explain: As the algae died and decomposed, they consumed dissolved oxygen in the water, leading to anoxic conditions that eventually caused the extinctions.

items.prompt: Is there a sharp line that separates the Big Five from all the other extinction events?

options.label: No; they appear to be among the largest on a smooth continuum
Yes; each of the five stands far above every other event
Yes; they are the only events that killed marine species
No; the Big Five are all exactly the same size

items.explain: The Big Five cannot be so clearly defined, but appear to represent the largest of a relatively smooth continuum of extinction events.
